headline: EU Politician Investigating Spyware Hacked With Pegasus
summary: A member of the European Parliament's PEGA committee, tasked with investigating spyware abuses, was targeted with Pegasus spyware. The hack occurred during his investigation and ahead of a key report.
details: Security researchers have confirmed that a European politician, Stelios Kouloglou, had his phone compromised with Pegasus spyware in 2022 and 2023. Kouloglou was a member of the European Parliament's PEGA committee, which was investigating abuses of such surveillance tools.

This marks the first time a member of the PEGA committee has been publicly identified as a victim of spyware. Kouloglou described the incident as "reckless" and a "direct attack on the rule of law," calling for stricter limits on spyware use across the EU.

The hacking occurred using a "zero-click" exploit that compromised a vulnerability in Apple's iPhone software. The spyware gained access without any interaction from Kouloglou, stealing private data including messages, location, and photos.

The timing of the hacks, in October 2022 and March 2023, coincided with the committee's discussions and Kouloglou's travel for hearings. Researchers did not attribute the hack to a specific country but noted the reuse of an email address previously used in campaigns against journalists.
Kouloglou plans to sue NSO Group, the Israeli company that develops Pegasus spyware. NSO Group has faced international scrutiny and sanctions for its role in facilitating government surveillance.

headline_marked: [[Tiered models]] separate public and private AI capabilities
headline: Tiered models separate public and private AI capabilities
summary: A new framework allows a single open-weight model to function with distinct public and private branches, controlled by a secret key.
details: A novel Tiered Language Model (TLM) framework introduces a method to integrate both public and private AI capabilities within a single open-weight model. This architecture splits the network into public and private branches, with a secret key directing computation through the private sub-graph, thereby hiding advanced features from users without the key.

This approach shifts capability control from post-hoc filtering to the model's core design. Unlike traditional methods that either prune dangerous functions or hide models behind closed APIs, TLM offers a unified weight set that can operate in multiple configurations without altering the base parameters.

The framework trains a public configuration that functions as a standard LLM, while a keyed configuration unlocks additional skills. Notably, the keyed configuration achieves perfect recall of private facts, with its specific parameters remaining at zero throughout training, ensuring a clear separation of functionalities.

Security is maintained as the secret key affects only about 5% of the model's parameters, making it resistant to fine-tuning-based extraction. However, current experiments are limited to smaller models, and the scalability to billions of parameters remains unproven. A full leak of the secret key would expose all private branches.

If successful, this tiered approach could enable companies to release open-weight checkpoints with embedded intellectual property-protected capabilities, eliminating the need for separate, closed-service endpoints and redefining how proprietary LLM functionalities are protected.
